common_name: Festiva Maxima Peony (Classic Fragrant White Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with the pink eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; planting too deep is the most common reason this and other peonies fail to bloom. Introduced in 1851, Festiva Maxima is one of the oldest and most widely planted peony cultivars still in commerce, prized for its huge, extremely fragrant, double white flowers flecked with crimson at the petal centers, opening earlier than most peony cultivars. Set out grow-through peony rings or stakes in spring before the heavy flowers weigh the stems down, especially after rain. It requires a real winter chill to set buds and is not reliable south of zone 8; expect little bloom the first year or two while the clump establishes, with plants living and flowering for decades once mature.

common_name: Karl Rosenfield Peony (Deep Red Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and set a peony ring in place early in spring before growth fills in. Introduced in 1908 and still one of the best-selling red peonies grown, Karl Rosenfield produces enormous, fully double, deep crimson-red flowers with a light, fresh fragrance on strong, well-branched stems that generally need less staking than other doubles of similar size. It is a vigorous, disease-resistant, long-blooming selection well suited to cutting, holding its color well as flowers age. Like other Paeonia lactiflora cultivars it needs sustained winter chill to flower well and is best in zones 3–8; cut foliage to the ground each fall to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Duchesse de Nemours Peony (Fragrant Double White Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake or ring the strong stems before the heavy, fragrant blooms open. Bred in France in 1856 and still a benchmark white peony, Duchesse de Nemours opens creamy-yellow at the bud and matures to pure white with a strong, sweet lemon-tinged fragrance, on stems that hold up well to wind and rain compared to many older doubles. It is an early- to mid-season bloomer that forces well as a cut flower, often chosen by florists and wedding growers for its reliability and scent. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

Bred by Sam Wissing and introduced in 1964, Coral Charm opens a vivid coral-orange and fades gracefully through peach to soft cream-pink as each large, semi-double flower ages, so a single plant can show several shades at once during peak bloom. It is an early-season bloomer with strong, upright stems that rarely need staking, and it has become one of the most widely planted of the coral-toned peonies for its vigor and reliable performance. Full sun and excellent drainage are essential; wet feet in winter are more likely than heat to kill an established peony.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Bartzella is an intersectional (Itoh) hybrid, crossing herbaceous peony with tree peony parentage, bearing enormous, semi-double to double, clear lemon-yellow flowers with a faint red flare at the base of each petal and a light citrus fragrance. Unlike most herbaceous peonies its strong, woody-based stems hold the huge blooms upright without staking, and its foliage stays clean and attractive well after bloom into fall. Itoh hybrids tolerate more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight Paeonia lactiflora cultivars, performing reliably into zone 9 with some afternoon shade, and die back to the ground each winter like an herbaceous peony rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; single-flowered peonies like this one carry their blooms on notably sturdy stems and rarely need staking. Introduced in 1928, Krinkled White bears large, single, pure white flowers with crepe-paper-textured, ruffled petals surrounding a prominent boss of bright golden stamens, giving it a simpler, more naturalistic look than the double cultivars. Bees and other pollinators favor single peonies like this one for the open, accessible center, and the flowers are excellent, long-lasting cut blooms despite their delicate appearance. It blooms in midseason and is one of the most award-winning white single peonies in cultivation, valued for its garden-worthy habit as much as its flowers.

common_name: Bowl of Beauty Peony (Pink Japanese-Form Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a peony ring for support as the wide flowers open. Bowl of Beauty is a Japanese-form peony, with a single outer ring of broad, deep rose-pink guard petals surrounding a dense, contrasting bowl of creamy-yellow staminodes, giving each flower a striking two-toned, bicolor effect unlike the fully double cultivars. It blooms in midseason on strong stems, is an outstanding, long-lasting cut flower, and its open form makes pollen and nectar more accessible to bees than fully double peonies. As with other Paeonia lactiflora cultivars, plants need a sustained winter chill to bloom well and are not reliable in zones 9 and warmer.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide only when clumps become overcrowded, since peonies otherwise thrive undisturbed for decades. Introduced in 1946, Do Tell is a Japanese-form peony with soft lavender-pink guard petals surrounding a full, ruffled center of narrow, cream-and-pink staminodes that give the bloom a frilly, two-toned appearance distinct from the fully double cultivars. It flowers in early-to-midseason on strong stems that generally stand up well without staking, and its lighter, more open form sheds rain better than heavy doubles. Like other lactiflora cultivars, it needs real winter cold to set buds and is best suited to zones 3–8.
